title: Claim the key first; the database decides who does the work
caption: One INSERT against a unique key replaces check-then-insert, so two concurrent retries can never both charge.

steps.text: Insert (key, request_hash, status = in_progress). The unique constraint means exactly one attempt can win.
Won the claim: do the side effect, then store status = done and the response. For a local write, do both in one transaction.
Lost the claim: first compare fingerprints. Same key with a different amount is a client bug, so refuse it instead of replaying the wrong answer.
Same request and already done: replay the stored response.
Same request still in progress (the first attempt is running): answer 409 so the client backs off and retries later.

scenarios.name: Two retries at once
scenarios.summary: Attempts A and B carry the same key 5 ms apart: the unique key lets exactly one INSERT win, and the loser sees in_progress and gets 409.

steps.text: A and B both try to INSERT key 7f3a at almost the same moment.
A's insert wins: it goes on to charge the card.
B's insert hits the unique constraint. Its body hash matches, so it's the same request.
A hasn't stored a response yet (status in_progress), so B gets 409 and retries later.
A finishes, stores status done with its response and returns it. B's next retry is a replay.

scenarios.name: Same key, new body
scenarios.summary: 7f3a already paid $30; a request with 7f3a and $45 fails the fingerprint check and gets 422, never a replayed $30 response.

steps.text: A request with key 7f3a and amount $45 arrives; the INSERT conflicts with the existing row.
Lost the claim, so compare request hashes: the stored one is for $30.
Different body: answer 422. Checking the hash before the status means a reused key is caught even while the first request is running.

scenarios.name: Alternative: check, then insert
scenarios.summary: Look the key up, do the work, insert the key last: two retries both read 'not found' in between and both charge, and a crash before the insert loses the key. Only a claim-first unique insert closes both gaps.

steps.text: A and B (the same request, 5 ms apart) both SELECT the key.
Neither has inserted it yet, so both read 'not found'.
Both charge the card: $60 for one checkout.
Worse, if the process dies between the charge and the INSERT, the key is never stored, and even a much later retry charges again.
